{{short description|Swiss mathematician}}
[[File:Anna Barbara Reinhart, Schweizer Mathematikerin (1730-1796).jpg|thumb|Copper engraving of Anna Reinhart]]
[[File:Anna Barbara Reinhart, Schweizer Mathematikerin (1730-1796), vier Ansichten.jpg|thumb|4 images of Anna Reinhart, unknown artist]]
'''Anna Barbara Reinhart''' (12 July 1730 – 5 January 1796), was a Swiss mathematician. She was considered an internationally respected mathematician of her era.

== Biography ==
Anna Barbara Reinhart was the third child and first daughter of Councilor Salomon Reinhart (1693 - 1761) and Anna Steiner.<ref>Rudolf Wolf: ETH-Bibliothek Zürich / Biographien zur Kulturgeschichte... [358.] In: Biographien zur Kulturgeschichte der Schweiz. Retrieved 4 June 2017 {{in lang |de}}.</ref>

Her childhood was overshadowed by an accident when she fell off her horse at a wedding party, which caused her to be confined her to her bed for significant periods of time.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Reinhart, Barbara, Mathematikerin, 1730-1796 - Winterthur Glossar|url=https://www.winterthur-glossar.ch/app/default/pub/fw.action/article?ce_id=165&ce_name=Person|access-date=2020-06-23|website=www.winterthur-glossar.ch|archive-date=2018-08-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180820173344/https://www.winterthur-glossar.ch/app/default/pub/fw.action/article?ce_id=165&ce_name=Person|url-status=dead}}</ref> Her physician, Dr. Johann Heinrich Hegner, however, noticed her aptitude for mathematics and began to teach her.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Reinhart, Anna Barbara|url=https://hls-dhs-dss.ch/articles/026116/2011-11-08/|access-date=2020-06-23|website=hls-dhs-dss.ch|language=de}}</ref> Henceforth, she studied mathematics using the books of [[Leonhard Euler]], [[Gabriel Cramer]], [[Pieter van Musschenbroek]] and [[Jérôme Lalande]].

Reinhart corresponded with several mathematicians of the period, such as [[Christoph Jezler]], and also received them as guests. She was active as a teacher of mathematics and was the instructor of [[Ulrich Hegner]] and [[Heinrich Bosshard von Rümikon]] among others. It is said that she edited the works of several of her contemporaries and wrote a manuscript commenting on the ''[[Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica]]'' by [[Isaac Newton]],<ref>{{Cite web|date=1858|title=1 (1858) Biographien zur Kulturgeschichte der Schweiz. 1. Cyclus / von Rudolf Wolf|url=http://www.e-rara.ch/zut/3598134|access-date=2020-06-23|website=www.e-rara.ch|language=en}}</ref> however her comments were lost after her death, but her letters to Christoph Jezler were preserved.<ref name=":0" />

Several contemporaries commended Reinhart in their work, such as [[Daniel Bernoulli]] who praised her for expanding and improving the [[Pursuit curve|pursuit curve]] as discussed by [[Pierre Louis Maupertuis]].

Reinhart died in 1796 at the age of 66 from gout and the consequences of her childhood accident, from which never fully recovered.

==Legacy==
In 2003, a street was named after her in her hometown [[Winterthur]] in [[Zürich|Zurich, Switzerland]].
